newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - 'Phantom' wartime bombers haunt the English moors.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - 'Phantom' wartime bombers haunt the English moors.

text.p: A trail of twisted wreckage lies strewn across the wind-swept hilltop, largely undisturbed in the 50 years since a desperate American pilot struggled to pull his plane just a few feet higher.
In a fiery flash the B-29 Superfortress slammed into the bog-soaked moor, killing Captain Landon Tanner and his 12-man crew.

Lying between the big urban centres of Sheffield and Manchester, the cluster of rugged, heather clad hills, known as the Dark Peaks, cuts northern England in two and has become a graveyard for aircraft. The weather changes almost by the minute and a jagged peak can suddenly be shrouded in fog or low clouds.
The hills have claimed more than 50 planes and more than 100 lives, many in the months after World War Two when jubilant young pilots eagerly awaited their trip home.
And according to reports circulating in this region, some local residents think the pilots may still be trying to get there.
BRITAIN'S BERMUDA TRIANGLE

Stories abound of World War Two-era planes suddenly appearing on the moors, only to vanish without trace. Some people speak of a local version of the notorious 'Bermuda Triangle', a mysterious region where travellers can suddenly vanish.

Late one evening in March this year two independent calls to South Yorkshire police reported a low-flying aircraft that appeared to be losing altitude. Several minutes later a local game keeper phoned to say he and his wife had seen a bright flash and heard an explosion on a nearby moor.

After the third call the police went into action, launching a search and rescue mission with two helicopters, 150 trained mountain rescuers, and dogs. The hunt across the bleak landscape continued through the night.
But the police found nothing. No plane was reported lost and no local airfield or flying club had logged a flight there.

"We went out and did an immediate search because people were so convinced they had seen something," said a local police spokesman. The police were looking for something real. "There was no question of a possible ghost or anything like that."

Phil Shaw, head of the mountain rescue group, said one of those who called was a former pilot. "He knew what he was talking about. There was a real plane flying that night that might not have been logged. The pilot must have been lost."

Teacher Judith Oldroyd lives in the village of Edale, whose stone cottages nestle in a valley below the Dark Peaks. She recounted the experience of her 82-year-old mother, a practical woman "not given to fanciful stories".

The mother returned from her usual walk that same day in March and immediately called her daughter to say she had seen a bomber buzzing right overhead and that it suddenly went silent and disappeared.

"When I told her it must have flown over a hill, she said 'I spent the war watching for those planes, I know what I saw'," said Oldroyd, explaining that her mother did not want to be named for fear of being thought 'crazy'.

Several days later Oldroyd was astonished to read of the nearby 'ghost plane' incident that set off the rescue effort. "Clearly someone has one of those old bombers and enjoys buzzing the villages in the area. I don't believe in phantom planes."
THINGS THAT GO BUMP IN THE NIGHT
Just over the hill from where the B-29 crashed, a 21-year-old Canadian pilot, Captain Anthony Clifford, and five crewmen met death when their Lancaster bomber went down on May 18, 1945.
Having flown its final mission over Germany two weeks earlier with a bombing raid on Hitler's home at Berechtesgarden, the crew was about to return home to Canada.

The Lancaster's flight path and time of day of its crash matched that of the March's bizarre incident. But historian Ron Collier, who has studied the Peak District's crash sites for 30 years and written two books on them, brushes aside such coincidence.
"These sightings always happen at night. If it were during the day, no one would even notice. It's as though things go bump in the dark."

He speculates that the pilot may have been trying to navigate by the nearby roads and that the explosion could have been from one of the many wartime grenades that hikers still occassionally find unexploded in the hills.
"Whoever it was, he was crazy to fly like that."
Collier explains that many of the wrecks in the area occurred just after the war when pilots celebrating their imminent return home let down their guard.
American pilots stationed at local airbases were particularly at risk because they hated flying in the clouds, a near constant in the damp, harsh climate of the northern moors.
"They always liked to fly 'contact', to fly low enough to see the ground," Collier explained. "That often proved fatal."
Another dangerous tendency was to circle over the homes of girlfriends of the crew. "At the time people thought Clifford may have been doing just that," Collier said.
THE SILENT FORCE

Several minutes after dismissing claims of phantom bombers as nonsense, the amateur historian became quiet. "I haven't spoken of this to anyone, but several weeks ago a friend and I were walking near an old airfield late one evening and suddenly a plane came over the hedge and vanished.
"I could just glimpse the back and a tail light. There was no noise at all. I don't know what it was. We didn't say a word to one another until the next day."
Several sightings were reported recently by people looking for the Hale-Bopp comet that could be seen in the night skies at the time.

According to the national Daily Mail newspaper, Mariafrance Tatersfield, a former special constable, watched a plane vanish over the moors. "It was flying very low as if to come in to land and then disappeared behind some trees. It's mind-boggling," she said.
Such sightings have not just occurred recently. Two years ago postman Tony Ingle was walking his golden retriever when he saw a bomber coming down a hill and banking to the left.

"There was an eerie silence. It looked like it was going to crash. I saw it as plain as anything. But when we ran over to it, there was nothing there. I don't really believe in ghosts, but I saw it as sure as day."

Collier occassionally leads groups into the hills to visit some of the wrecks. People often grow quiet as they approach and see the debris slowly rusting where it landed so many years ago. Some plant makeshift wooden crosses at the sites, which have become a sort of shrine.
"There may not be ghosts, but there is a kind of force that seems to surround these sites. A lot of boys died here."
